The Guardian: Few fixtures in European football carry the weight of the Primeira Liga Clássico, and Sunday's encounter at the Estádio do Dragão did nothing to diminish that reputation. Porto arrived in dominant form and played accordingly, pressing Benfica relentlessly from the first whistle, with Galeno the central tormentor on the left flank. The Brazilian winger was Porto's most dangerous outlet throughout the opening period, repeatedly driving inside, winning duels at will and drawing the fouls that disrupted Benfica's rhythm before it could establish itself. His most telling contribution came in the build-up to the opener: a winding run that drew two defenders before the ball was recycled to Taremi, who dispatched it low into the far corner on 38 minutes with characteristic composure.

Benfica spent the first 45 minutes struggling to cope with a press that was both high and meticulously organised. Their attempts to play from the back were consistently disrupted; Otamendi and António Silva could barely complete two passes before Porto's forwards arrived at speed. Trubin made a critical save from Evanilson's close-range effort on 27 minutes — the one moment that kept Benfica alive going into the break — but the visitors had created almost nothing of their own.

Sky Sports: The second half was a different match, and much of the credit belongs to Schmidt's half-time restructuring. Benfica shifted to a more direct approach that bypassed Porto's compact midfield press with longer balls from Trubin. Di María, introduced on 62 minutes, was the difference the change required. Five minutes after arriving he threaded the pass that Rafa Silva converted calmly for the equaliser, and from that moment Porto looked unsettled, their defensive shape — so reliable for an hour — beginning to fragment under pressure.
